title: Erase AB and CD Pairs
statement:
You get a string s of uppercase English letters. In one move you may delete any occurrence of the two-letter piece "AB" or "CD". The remaining parts join together, and that can create a new pair that you may delete in a later move.

Make as many moves as you like. Return the shortest length s can reach.

examples.why: Delete "AB" to get "CDA". Now C and D touch, so delete "CD" too. Only "A" is left.
"BA" and "DC" are the pairs in the wrong order. Nothing can be deleted.
The pairs are nested: deleting the inner "CD" exposes another "CD", and then "AB". A single left-to-right replace would stop at "ACDB".

hints: Deleting a pair can bring two letters together that were apart. Which letters can meet that way?
When you read a B, it can be deleted together with the closest letter to its left that has not been deleted yet, if that letter is A. Which structure always gives you that letter?
Push letters onto a stack. Before pushing a B, check whether the top is A; before pushing a D, check whether the top is C. If so, pop instead of pushing. The answer is the stack's size.

explain.intuition:
Read the string left to right and keep what has survived so far. When the next letter is B, the only letter it can ever pair with is the last surviving letter before it: everything between them is already gone. If that letter is A, delete both. The same goes for D and C. "The last surviving letter" is exactly the top of a stack.

It is the same shape as matching brackets: A and C are opening brackets, B and D close them. Deleting greedily never hurts, because a pair that can be deleted now stays deletable no matter what else you remove, so the order of moves does not change the final length.
steps: For each letter c of s: if c is B and the top is A, or c is D and the top is C, pop the top.
pitfalls: Doing one replace pass. Deletions expose new pairs, as in "ACCDDB"; you need to repeat until nothing changes, which is O(n²) on deeply nested input.
Matching the pairs in either order. "BA" and "DC" are not deletable.
Mixing up the partners, for example letting D cancel an A. "ADCB" stays at 4 letters.

solutions.title: Delete until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Remove every AB and CD, and repeat while the string keeps shrinking.

solutions.title: Stack of surviving letters
solutions.idea: A closing letter cancels the top of the stack when it is its partner; otherwise it is pushed.

followups: Return the final string itself, not just its length. What changes?
The deletable pairs are given as a list of any two-letter strings, for example also "BC". Does the stack approach still give the shortest result, and why or why not?
lcTitle: Minimum String Length After Removing Substrings
